newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says Mobutu regime in Zaire is over.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Mobutu regime in Zaire is over.

text.p: Top Clinton administration officials said on Tuesday that President Mobutu Sese Seko's regime was at an end but said they still hoped he would work for a political settlement of Zaire's civil war.
"It is clear that Mobuto, the Mobuto regime is a thing of the past," U.S. Assistant Secretary of State George Moose told a congressional hearing.
"The question is how is it going to be replaced," the State Department's head of African affairs told a House International Affairs subcommittee hearing.

"It is a movement to a post-Mobutu scene ... how he departs the scene is important. Mr. Mobuto could play a positive role" in dealing with the alliance led by rebel leader Laurent Kabila, which is rapidly gaining ground.
Moose said that talks between the two sides in South Africa have been adjourned for the time being, but he predicted there would be further political negotiations.
"Even if they (the rebel alliance) were to prevail militarily," Moose said, "they recognise there has to be a political settlement."

Rebel forces have seized nearly a third of Zaire as Mobutu's troops flee or even switch sides, including important mining areas. They appear on the verge of capturing Zaire's second largest city, Lubumbashi, a Defence Department expert told the panel.
Mobuto on Tuesday declared a state of emergency in Zaire, appointing military governors to provinces not under rebel control.

"The pattern has been that as the alliance moves toward a town, the FAZ (government army) troops flee after looting," said Vincent Kern, the Pentagon's top Africa expert. "The major reason for the success is not so much the competence of the alliance, but the weakness of the FAZ," he said.
Kern said the rebels appear poised to capture the mineral-rich Shaba province, gains he attributed more to popular support and FAZ incompetence than to outside help.
He dismissed claims by Mobutu and others in Europe that rebel gains came because of help from Uganda and Rwanda, although neighbouring countries did provide training and weapons to the rebels.
"There is no evidence that leads us to believe that either organised Ugandan or Rwandan units were fighting with or directing the alliance," Kern said.

The Pentagon has sent 1,400 Marines on the U.S. helicopter landing ship Nassau to stand by for a possible evacuation of about 450 Americans and possibly other foreign nationals. Kern said about 100 of the Marines are taking control of evacuation force headquarters at Brazzaville from Army and Air Force personnel, but no decision has been made on an evacuation.
"We have absolutely no intention of intervening in the Zairean conflict or using our forces to influence the events in Zaire," Kern said. "We have no strategic interests in Zaire."
